opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one I was thinking about a lot when I made the shift to working on medical AI full-time.

When I started, there was this striking mismatch. On one hand, you had general-purpose language models that were clearly picking up a surprising amount of medical knowledge just from pre-training on the web. You could ask them clinical questions and sometimes get answers that were genuinely impressive. On the other hand, almost none of that was showing up in actual care delivery. Clinicians weren't using these tools in any systematic way, health systems weren't deploying them, and patients certainly weren't getting the benefit in a reliable, trustworthy form.

The way I framed the gap was roughly in three layers. The first was capability: were the models actually good enough on the things that matter clinically, not just trivia-style recall but reasoning, knowing when they're uncertain, avoiding harmful answers? The second was evaluation: even if a model was capable, we didn't have good ways to measure that convincingly. Multiple-choice benchmarks are useful as a starting signal, but they don't tell you whether a model's long-form answer to a real patient question is safe, complete, and aligned with clinical consensus. The third was everything around deployment: workflow integration, regulation, liability, trust, and the very reasonable conservatism of a field where mistakes hurt people.

My sense at the time was that the field had been somewhat stuck because people were treating these as separate problems. Researchers would push a number on a benchmark, and then there'd be this big leap of faith to say, "therefore it's ready for clinical use." So a lot of what motivated the early work was trying to close the evaluation gap first. If you can build evaluations that clinicians actually find meaningful, with human raters, careful rubrics, and comparisons against physician answers, then you create a shared language between the AI community and the medical community. That makes the capability progress legible and gives you a much more credible path toward responsible adoption.

I was also fairly optimistic, maybe more than some people, that the capability side would move faster than expected. Scaling plus targeted alignment for the medical domain seemed likely to close a lot of the gap quickly. So I thought the bottleneck would increasingly shift toward the human and systems side: how do you design these tools so they actually help clinicians and patients, and how do you build the evidence base so the healthcare system can trust them? That's still largely how I think about it today.

r001.rationale: The response separates proving clinical capability and safety through meaningful evaluation from the deployment, trust, and adoption challenges faced by healthcare systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I came to this from a slightly unusual angle. I'd been working on these models at Google, and around the time we were doing the early Med-PaLM work, the thing that struck me wasn't really that the models couldn't do medical reasoning. We were seeing them pass USMLE-style questions, we were seeing them give explanations that physicians would actually rate favorably in blinded comparisons. The capability was clearly arriving, and arriving faster than I think most people in healthcare expected.

The gap, as I saw it, was almost entirely on the other side. Healthcare is a domain where the cost of being wrong is asymmetric, the people who'd use these tools are overworked and skeptical for very good reasons, and the institutions have decades of hard-earned caution baked into how they adopt anything. So you had this situation where the technology was moving on a timescale of months and the adoption machinery was built to move on a timescale of years.

And I think a lot of people in AI looked at that and said, well, the problem is regulation, or the problem is that doctors are conservative. I didn't really buy that framing. The honest version is that we hadn't yet done the work to earn trust. A model that's right ninety percent of the time on a benchmark isn't a product. You need to understand the failure modes, you need to understand how it behaves with the messy, incomplete, contradictory information that real patients actually present with, and you need to have thought carefully about where a human stays in the loop and why.

So when I decided to go full-time on this, the way I thought about it was: capability is close to a solved problem relative to the other pieces. The interesting work is in the translation layer. How do you evaluate these systems in ways that clinicians actually find credible? How do you design the interaction so that the model is augmenting judgment instead of replacing it in ways that nobody signed up for? How do you deal with the fact that medicine isn't one task, it's thousands of tasks with very different risk profiles?

And honestly, I also thought the gap was an opportunity, not just an obstacle. There's a real chance here to improve access to care for people who currently have very little of it. If you can close that gap thoughtfully, the upside is enormous. So I wasn't discouraged by it. I just thought it needed people who were willing to sit in the uncomfortable middle between the research and the clinic for a long time.

r001.rationale: The candidate separates growing model capability from clinical adoption and says benchmark performance alone is not enough: systems must demonstrate credible evaluation, understood failure modes, and safe human oversight to earn trust for clinical use.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was that those were really two different problems. You could have a model that knew a lot of medicine and performed well on an exam, but that didn’t automatically mean it could help a doctor or a patient in practice. An exam gives you a fairly well-defined question. In healthcare, figuring out what question to ask, what information is missing, and when you need to defer to someone else is a huge part of the work.

So I thought about the gap as both a research problem and a deployment problem. We needed to improve the models, but we also needed to understand the workflows they would fit into and build evidence that they actually helped. Can a clinician check the output efficiently? Does the system save time overall? Does it recognize when it doesn’t have enough information?

The exciting thing was that you didn’t necessarily need to automate an entire doctor’s job to make a meaningful difference. There are narrower tasks where helping someone understand information or reducing administrative work could be valuable. But getting from an impressive demonstration to something people can reliably use was going to require a lot of careful work with the people delivering care.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes model capability from practical deployment and discusses building evidence for reliable use, but it does not clearly separate persuading the healthcare community that LLMs are viable from establishing their trustworthiness for clinical use.

sol-6.1.text:
When I started working on medical AI full-time, the thing that stood out was how big the gap was between what these models could do in a research setting and what was actually useful in a clinical workflow. You could get an impressive answer to a medical question, but that didn’t automatically mean you had something a doctor could safely rely on while caring for a patient.

I thought of that as both an opportunity and a research problem. What evidence would make someone comfortable using this? How do you evaluate performance on the messy cases that show up in practice? And how do you fit it into a workflow so that it actually saves time or improves care?

So the goal wasn’t just to make a model that knew more medicine. It was to understand what was missing between a capable model and a useful system. In healthcare, that last stretch involves reliability, evaluation, and trust, as much as raw capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between model capability and safe, reliable clinical use, including trust and evaluation. It does not clearly distinguish healthcare professionals viewing LLMs as viable from establishing their trustworthiness for clinical use.
